details:
**The Little Mermaid statue**
Edvard Eriksen's 1913 bronze sculpture of the title character of Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale, sitting on a rock by the Langelinie promenade in the harbor near the Kastellet fortress. It was commissioned by Carlsberg brewing heir Carl Jacobsen and partly modeled on ballerina Ellen Price. The statue has been vandalized many times and beheaded more than once. It is the most common giveaway for the city.

**Tivoli Gardens**
One of the world's oldest amusement parks, opened in 1843 in the city center. Walt Disney visited it, and it influenced his design of Disneyland. It contains the Rutschebanen, a wooden roller coaster from 1914.

**Øresund Bridge and Malmö**
The Øresund Bridge, opened in 2000, is part of a combined bridge and tunnel link that carries road and rail traffic across the Øresund strait. It connects Copenhagen to Malmö, Sweden.

**Zealand and Amager islands**
Copenhagen lies mostly on the east coast of Zealand (Sjælland), Denmark's largest island, and partly on the smaller island of Amager. The inner harbor runs between the two.

**Amalienborg Palace**
The main residence of the Danish royal family, made up of four identical palaces around an octagonal square. Jacques Saly's equestrian statue of King Frederick V stands at the square's center.

**Noma and René Redzepi**
Noma is chef René Redzepi's restaurant, famous for "New Nordic" cuisine built on foraged local ingredients. Restaurant magazine has named it the best restaurant in the world several times. The city is also home to Geranium, a top-rated restaurant located in the Parken national stadium.

**Kastellet and the Gefion Fountain**
Kastellet is a well-preserved star-shaped 17th-century citadel near the harbor, close to the Little Mermaid. The nearby Gefion Fountain shows the Norse goddess Gefjon driving her four sons, changed into oxen, to plow the island of Zealand out of Sweden, as the myth tells. Carlsberg funded the fountain.

**Finger Plan**
A 1947 urban plan that guided Copenhagen's growth along five "fingers" of rail-served development that spread out from a central "palm," with green wedges left open between them.

**Freetown Christiania**
A self-proclaimed autonomous commune founded in 1971 by squatters on a former military base in the Christianshavn area. Its "Pusher Street" was long known for openly selling cannabis.

**smørrebrød**
Traditional Danish open-faced sandwiches on rye bread. They are served at famous spots such as Restaurant Ida Davidsen, known for its huge menu, and by bakery chains such as Ole & Steen (Lagkagehuset).

**Battle of Copenhagen (1801) and 1807 bombardment**
In the 1801 naval battle, Horatio Nelson ignored Admiral Hyde Parker's signal to withdraw, supposedly by "turning a blind eye" to it. In 1807, a British bombardment that used Congreve rockets set much of the city on fire, and the British then seized the Danish fleet.

**Strøget**
The city's long car-free pedestrian shopping street, which runs from City Hall Square to Kongens Nytorv. It is promoted as one of the longest pedestrian streets in Europe.

**Carlsberg**
The famous Danish brewery, founded in Copenhagen in 1847, which still has its historic site in the city. Members of the Jacobsen brewing family funded many city landmarks, including the Little Mermaid and the Gefion Fountain.

**Christiansborg and Rosenborg palaces**
Christiansborg Palace, on the islet of Slotsholmen, houses the Danish Parliament (Folketing), the Prime Minister's office, and the Supreme Court. Rosenborg Castle, a Renaissance palace built by Christian IV, holds the Danish crown jewels.

**2009 UN Climate Change Conference (COP15)**
The 2009 United Nations climate summit was held in Copenhagen. It produced the non-binding Copenhagen Accord rather than a full treaty.
